Um, well, with my friends and family, it's mostly just them getting a little exasperated because I keep asking them to look at my photos, but at work... yeah, it's definitely starting to cause some real friction with my coworkers and my boss. 

Like, just last week, for example, we were putting together the final promotional packets and event materials for this upcoming tech convention. It’s a really big deal for our agency. I was supposed to send the digital proofs over to the printer by 3 PM on Thursday. But the packet included these team photos from our last major event, and I just... I couldn't stop looking at my face in them. The asymmetry was just screaming at me. I sat there at my desk, and I kept zooming in, trying to see if I could crop it differently, or maybe adjust the contrast so the shadows didn't highlight the unevenness so much. I even tried swapping out the photo for an older one, but then the formatting of the whole page got completely messed up, and I had to try and fix that. Before I even realized what was happening, it was almost 5 PM, and I completely missed the planning deadline for the print run. My boss had to call the printing company and literally beg them to squeeze our order in, and she was so confused and frustrated with me because usually I'm so on top of my schedule.

And it's not just that one time, either. It's bleeding into my everyday tasks. Like, vendor calls used to be so quick—I'd just hop on a video call, finalize the floral arrangements or the AV setup, and be done in ten or fifteen minutes. But now, because I know they can see me on the camera, meeting prep takes me so much longer than it should. I spend at least twenty or thirty minutes before every single call just adjusting my webcam, moving my desk lamp around, trying to find an angle that hides how lopsided my face looks. And then during the call, I'm just staring at my little video square the entire time instead of looking at the vendor's presentation. Everything just takes me longer now. My coworkers are definitely starting to notice that I'm dragging my feet on things that used to take me no time at all, and I hate it. I really do. I worked so hard to get this job right out of high school, and I don't want them to think I'm slacking off, but I just get so paralyzed trying to manage how I look in these materials and on these calls.

I came in because I cannot stop staring at this one specific part of my face in every single picture. It's just so uneven-looking. Like, incredibly uneven. I spend, I don't even know how long, just zooming in on my phone and staring at it, trying to figure out how to hide it or why it looks like that. I've pointed it out to my friends, my coworkers, literally anyone I feel comfortable enough to ask, and they all tell me they barely see anything, or that it looks completely normal. But I know what I'm seeing! It's just right there, and ever since I started having to be in front of people more at work, it's all I can focus on. It's completely ruining how I feel when I'm supposed to be running an event, and I just... I can't let it go, no matter what anyone says to me.\n\nDoctor: Is it just your appearance that's been bothering you, or are there other things that you've been worrying about or feeling are not right?\n\nPatient: Um, no, not really. Well, that's the thing, and honestly, that's kind of the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because if you ask them, they all say no. It just makes me feel like I'm completely losing my mind, because to me it's this huge, undeniable flaw, but they swear up and down they barely notice it.

Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess I hear what you're saying, and I know that's exactly what my mom and Maya and everyone else is trying to tell me when they say they don't see it. But... how could it just be my perception? Like, when I wake up in the morning and go into my bathroom—I have this specific mirror in there, I actually installed these bright LED vanity lights around it last year when I moved into this apartment because I wanted good lighting for doing my makeup before work—when I stand there, it is just... it's right there. But then ten minutes later I'll be in the kitchen heating up my morning coffee, and I'll catch my reflection in the dark glass of the microwave door, or later I'll see myself in the window of the subway when we're going through a tunnel on my commute to the office, and my heart just completely drops all over again. Because it looks so undeniably real. It's not like some optical illusion I'm making up in my brain. It's my actual physical face. 

So, I mean, I really wish I could believe it was just my perception, because honestly that would be so much easier, wouldn't it? If I could just snap my fingers and suddenly see a normal, even face like everyone else supposedly sees. But I just don't see how it could be in my head when it's staring right back at me every single time I look.

If I could just fix this unevenness, or if it just didn't look so glaringly obvious, everything would be completely perfect. \n\nBut instead, it just takes up all my mental energy. Like, even just yesterday, I was supposed to be finalizing a catering menu for a huge corporate retreat—like 300 people, lots of moving parts—and instead of focusing on the dietary restrictions spreadsheet like I needed to, I spent, I don't know, maybe forty-five minutes in the venue's bathroom mirror just staring at how the overhead lighting caught my face. I was trying to see if the fluorescent lights made the asymmetry look worse than it did in the photos we took last week. So, yeah, it's really just the way I look that's wrong. Everything else in my life is completely fine, I just can't enjoy it because of this.\n\nDoctor: Has your focus on this unevenness on your face affected your relationships with friends, family, or coworkers?\n\nPatient: Um, well, with my friends and family, it's mostly just them getting a little exasperated because I keep asking them to look at my photos, but at work... yeah, it's definitely starting to cause some real friction with my coworkers and my boss. \n\nLike, just last week, for example, we were putting together the final promotional packets and event materials for this upcoming tech convention. I mean... no. Honestly, no. And I know I keep bringing this up, and I know I probably sound like a completely broken record today, but... that is exactly why I came in to see you in the first place. Because it *is* there. 

Like I was just saying about the whole shift at work—going from being safely behind a desk doing data entry to suddenly being the one out there handing out lanyards and greeting the VIPs—ever since that happened, I just cannot stop staring at this one uneven-looking part of my face in all the event photos. I just... I can't accept that it's not there. It has to be there, because I'm looking right at it. I'm not hiding in my room or anything, I'm still seeing everyone, but I guess I'm not really enjoying it the way I used to because I'm just so hyper-focused on how I look in every single situation where a camera might come out or where someone might be looking at me too closely.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your face are interfering with your ability to perform your job as an event planner?\n\nPatient: Yeah, definitely. I mean, like I was kind of saying before with the whole webcam thing, it’s really starting to get in the way. It’s... well, it’s a lot of little things that just add up. Like, before I send out any event pictures for our client wrap-up reports, or even right before I join one of those vendor meetings, I just... I can't help it, I'll pull out my phone and open the front-facing camera. And I'll just sit at my desk checking my face over and over. \n\nI'll tilt my head a certain way, you know, just trying to find an angle where the unevenness doesn't look so completely obvious in the office lighting. And if we need to send reference photos of the venue setup that I happen to be in, I'll literally retake the photos a million times until I find one where my face doesn't look completely wrong. Or sometimes I get so stuck in my own head about it that I'll turn to Maya—she's the other junior coordinator who sits in the pod next to me—and I'll just flat out ask her if I look weird. I'll be like, \"Maya, be honest, does this side of my jaw look super lopsided today?\" And she's really sweet about it, but I know it puts her in an awkward position, and I know I ask her way too much. \n\nBut I just get so trapped in this loop of checking my phone camera, tilting my head, asking Maya for reassurance... and it can just eat up so much time. Like, enough time that I'm actually starting to fall behind on my real planning stuff. The event timelines, the budget spreadsheets, following up with the linen rental places... those tasks just sit there on my desk while I'm obsessing over my phone screen. It's so frustrating because I know I have a million things to do, and event planning is all about time management, but it's like my brain won't let me move on to the actual work until I feel okay about how I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that others can see the unevenness in your face as clearly as you can?\n\nPatient: Well, that's the thing, and honestly, that's kind of the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because if you ask them, they all say no. Everyone else says they barely see anything at all, or they'll give me these generic lines like, \"Oh, nobody's face is perfectly symmetrical,\" which just feels like they're trying to placate me, you know? But to me, it is so glaringly obvious. \n\nIt’s just gotten so much worse lately because I’ve had to be more in front of people at work. When I first started at the agency right out of high school, I was mostly just doing behind-the-scenes stuff—data entry, organizing the supply closet, confirming catering numbers over email, stuff like that where nobody really had to look at me. It just makes me feel like I'm completely losing my mind, because to me it's this huge, undeniable flaw, but they swear up and down they barely notice it.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think that maybe your face looks fine and it's just your own perception that there's something wrong with it?\n\nPatient: Um... no, not really. I mean... I guess I get why you’re asking that, especially since I already told you that everyone else says they barely see anything at all. But... no, I really don't think it's possible that a plastic surgeon wouldn't see it. A plastic surgeon is completely different from my mom or my coworkers. Someone whose entire career is based on analyzing and fixing facial flaws? They would see it immediately.

Because if I sat in their chair, under those bright clinical lights, or if I showed them those exact same high-res photos I pull up on my couch every single night... they would see the shadow. They would see the unevenness right away. They wouldn't just brush it off and tell me I look fine like Maya does. I'm looking at regular mirrors, I'm looking at high-resolution digital photographs taken by professional photographers with DSLR cameras at these events. \n\nAnd like I was saying, I'll sit there on my couch—usually it's my gray sectional, I got it from IKEA, it's super comfortable but I just sink into it and get lost in my phone—and I'll pull up the gallery link the photographer sends us. And I look at the pictures of myself standing next to the floral arrangements or the registration desk, and it's right there. It's not like I'm projecting some internal feeling onto my face. I'm literally just observing what is physically present. \n\nI guess I just don't understand what you mean when you say my perception isn't based on how my face actually looks. Because my perception is literally *of* my face. When I zoom in on that one spot on my jaw, I'm looking at the actual pixels that make up the image of my face. I'm looking at the shadow that the uneven bone structure casts. It's not a feeling, it's a visual fact. So if my perception isn't based on how my face actually looks, then what is it based on? Because I'm not hallucinating. I know I'm not. I'm just looking really, really closely at something that everyone else is just glancing at. And when you look closely at something, you see the truth of it, right? You see the flaws that other people might miss when they're just walking past you in a busy convention hall. So, no, I just... I can't wrap my head around the idea that what I'm seeing isn't based on reality. It just doesn't make any sense to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your concerns about your face are impacting your overall quality of life?\n\nPatient: I mean... yeah. Honestly, yes, it really is. It’s bleeding into everything, especially my job, which is supposed to be the thing I’m actually good at. Like, just last week, I actually missed part of a major planning deadline. Which is so incredibly unlike me, because usually I am totally obsessed with my spreadsheets and my timelines, and I pride myself on keeping everything running smoothly. \n\nBut we got the proofs back for some of the new event materials—like the promotional flyers and the digital recap stuff we send out to the sponsors—and I happened to be in some of the shots from the registration table. And I just... I completely spiraled. I spent so much time dealing with how I looked in the event materials, just zooming in on my jaw, trying to figure out if I could get the graphic designer to crop me out or blur the background so it wouldn't look so obviously lopsided. The whole afternoon just vanished while I was agonizing over it, and I totally missed the cutoff to submit the finalized schedule to our director. \n\nAnd it’s not even just the big deadlines anymore, which is the really scary part. It’s the day-to-day stuff, too. Like, vendor calls and meeting prep take me so much longer than they should now. I used to just pick up the phone or walk into a meeting with the caterers or the AV team and just get straight to business. But now... if I have to prep for an in-person meeting, I'm spending twenty minutes in the office bathroom beforehand just trying to position my hair so it falls exactly right to hide that side of my face. Or if it's a video call with a vendor, I'm spending half an hour obsessing over the webcam angle and the ring light so the shadow doesn't highlight the unevenness. \n\nIt just... it takes up so much of my time and my mental energy. I feel like I'm doing two full-time jobs—my actual event planning job, and then this whole other exhausting job of just trying to manage my face and hide it from everyone. So, yeah, I guess it really is impacting my life. It's just making everything so much harder than it used to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that a doctor or a plastic surgeon would not see the unevenness you're describing if they examined your face in person?\n\nPatient: I mean... I guess I get why you’re asking that, especially since I already told you that everyone else says they barely see anything at all. Because if I sat in their chair, under those bright clinical lights, or if I showed them those exact same high-res photos I pull up on my couch every single night... they would see the shadow. They would see the unevenness right away. They wouldn't just brush it off and tell me I look fine like Maya does. They would look at my jaw and know exactly why I can't stop obsessing over it, because it is a physical reality that a trained professional would absolutely be able to spot.\n\nDoctor: Have you tried to hide or camouflage the unevenness on your face with makeup or other methods?\n\nPatient: Makeup... I mean, I try, but you can't really contour away an actual structural issue, you know? I’ve watched, like, dozens of YouTube tutorials on jawline contouring, and I've bought all these expensive matte bronzers, but it just looks like a muddy smudge on my face because the physical unevenness is still there underneath it. I'll have urgent emails piling up from the caterers or the venue managers, and I'm just sitting there staring at my phone camera, trying to fix how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Have you considered or actually consulted a dermatologist or plastic surgeon about the unevenness you see in your face?\n\nPatient: I haven't actually gone to see one, no. I mean, I've thought about it. I've thought about it a lot, actually, like I mentioned before when I was talking about looking up reviews online late at night. I've spent hours—like, literally hours—scrolling through RealSelf and Yelp and all these different plastic surgery forums, just trying to find someone who specializes in jaw asymmetry or facial reconstruction, just looking at their before-and-after galleries to see if they've fixed someone who looks like me. \n\nBut actually making the appointment? I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to do it. I mean... if I'm being completely honest with myself? I really don't think it would. I don't think their opinion would change anything for me. 

Because, honestly, that's kind of the whole reason I finally came in to see you in the first place. My role at work has been shifting lately, and I’ve had to be way more in front of people—like, actually out on the convention floor, interacting with the VIP clients, directing the catering staff face-to-face instead of just hiding behind my laptop in the back office. And because I'm out there so much more, I keep ending up in all these candid event photos that the hired photographers take for the promotional materials.

Is my jaw super obvious?\" I ask them so much, and they always just sigh and say no, but I just have to check. I can't help it.\n\nAnd honestly, doing all of this—the checking my phone camera, the retaking photos from a million angles, the tilting my head until my neck literally cramps, interrogating my coworkers about how I look—it just... it eats up so much time. Like I was saying earlier about missing that deadline, this is exactly why. I get so caught up in trying to camouflage it with my angles and checking my screen that an entire hour will just vanish, and I completely fall behind on my actual event planning stuff. I don't know. I guess anything is technically possible, but... it's just really hard for me to even wrap my head around that.
